title: On-call readiness and customer status framework for capacity blips
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

This document defines the operational workflow, runbook fragments, rotation templates, game‑day scenarios, and customer communication artifacts to handle short‑lived capacity blips across Redwood Inference (examples: Dedicated GPU pool saturation, KV cache eviction storms, router-proxy fan‑out exhaustion). It is focused on fast, coordinated mitigation and transparent customer communications with a priority on preservation of SLAs and minimizing customer confusion.

Scope

- Services in scope: redwood-runtime (inference workers), router-proxy, kv-cache-service, autoscaler, capacity-controller, metrics-exporter.
- Incident class: capacity blip. Defined as a sudden degradation in throughput/latency or elevated error rates directly attributed to resource exhaustion, autoscaler delays, or cache instability lasting >60s.
- Out of scope: data corruption, security incidents, or long-term performance regressions (handled by other processes).

Service targets and thresholds (Quick reference)

||Measurement||Target/Threshold||Responder||
|P95 latency (inference)|< 300 ms|Trigger: >= 350 ms for 3m|oncall-sre|
|Error rate (5m)|< 0.1%|Trigger: >= 0.5% for 5m|oncall-sre|
|Capacity headroom|>= 20%|Trigger: < 10% sustained for 5m|capacity-owner|
|KV cache eviction rate|< 100 evictions/s|Trigger: >= 300 evictions/s|runtime-owner|

Roles and responsibilities

- Primary responder (Tier 1): oncall-sre — initial triage, status updates, runbook execution.
- Secondary (Tier 2): runtime/backend owner — deeper diagnostics, config changes, rolling restarts.
- Capacity lead (Tier 3): infra-capacity — investigate autoscaler, provision additional Dedicated capacity if needed.
- Communications owner: customer-success on-call — customer-facing status and messages.
- Incident commander (IC): assigned for any incident that escalates to a major incident (see escalation ladder).

Rotation and staffing templates

1) Weekly on-call block (recommended for teams):
   - Primary: 1 engineer (Mon–Sun) with daily handoff at 09:00 UTC.
   - Secondary: dedicated backup (Mon–Fri 09:00–17:00 local).
   - Rotation length: 1 week.
2) Onboarding checklist for new oncall:
   - Verify PagerDuty & Slack routing.
   - Confirm access to production dashboards (Grafana), logs (Loki), traces (Tempo), and the status page editor.
   - Run the 20‑minute runbook drill (see Game day section).

Escalation ladder (capacity blip-specific)

1. Tier 1 (oncall-sre) handles detection and initial mitigation for up to 20 minutes.
2. If issue persists >20 minutes or visible customer impact increases, escalate to Tier 2 (runtime owner).
3. If autoscaling/provisioning is suspected or capacity headroom <5% and not remediated within 10 minutes after Tier 2 actions, notify Capacity Lead and assign an IC.
4. If there is multiple-region impact or major customer SLA breaches, declare Major Incident per incident-command-playbook and open an incident bridge.

Playbook: Capacity blip (step-by-step)

Goal: restore service to within SLOs and publish clear customer messaging within the first 15 minutes.

Immediate (0–5 min) — Triage and stabilize
1. Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty and open the incident channel (#inc-<service>-<id>).
2. Confirm the alert against Grafana dashboards: worker_utilization, queue_length, p95_latency, error_rate.
3. Record the following in the channel: time, top metrics, short hypothesis (e.g., GPU pool at 98% utilization).
4. Apply quick stabilizers if safe: temporarily increase request timeout, enable degraded routing (route to lower‑capacity variant), or scale down non‑critical batch jobs.

Commands and diagnostics (examples)
- Check worker pool utilization: kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=redwood-runtime -o wide
- Check autoscaler status: kubectl -n infra get hpa/autoscaler-capacity -o yaml
- Query KV cache evictions (PromQL): sum(rate(kv_cache_evictions_total[1m]))
- Review router queue depth: sum(rate(router_request_queue_size[1m])) by (region)

Mitigation (5–20 min) — targeted actions
1. If autoscaler latencies or limits cause the blip: trigger a manual scale-up via capacity-controller or provision reserved nodes in Dedicated. Document the command and reason in the incident channel.
2. If KV cache eviction storm: temporarily increase cache size by toggling cache-config (safe path) or apply conservative eviction policy.
3. If router-proxy exhaustion: reduce fan‑out by changing routing.weight to favor low‑fanout paths or enable circuit-breaker thresholds.
4. If misrouted traffic load: apply traffic shaping or re-route to healthy region.

Communication milestones

- T+5m: Post a short status to the internal incident channel describing scope and initial mitigations.
- T+15m: Publish a public status page message — “Investigating” with affected regions and impact.
- T+60m: Update status to “Mitigating” or “Identified” with ETA for next update.
- On resolution: publish root cause (summary), mitigation steps taken, and short-term work items.

Customer status page templates (copy/paste and customize)

Template variables: {SERVICE}, {IMPACT}, {REGIONS}, {ETA}, {WORKAROUND}

1) Investigating (first public message)
Title: {SERVICE} — Degraded performance in {REGIONS}
Body: We are aware of increased latency and reduced throughput affecting {SERVICE} in {REGIONS}. Our team is actively investigating. Customers may see elevated errors or timeouts; requests for short texts may be prioritized. We will provide an update by {ETA}.

2) Mitigating / Identified
Title: {SERVICE} — Mitigation in progress (root cause identified)
Body: We identified the primary cause as {IMPACT} and are applying targeted mitigations (manual scale-up, cache policy change). Affected customers should see improvement within {ETA}. If you are experiencing persistent issues, contact support@redwood.ai with your request IDs.

3) Resolved
Title: {SERVICE} — Resolved
Body: The incident impacting {REGIONS} has been resolved. Root cause: {IMPACT}. Immediate mitigation: {WORKAROUND}. Next steps: scheduled follow‑up fixes and capacity improvements. If you experienced customer-impacting events, our support team will reach out.

Use with Slack pinned summary and a short Tweet-style line for status page banners. Keep messages concise and avoid technical jargon for customer-facing updates.

Game day and 20-minute drills

Objective: exercise the 0–20 minute workflow, runbook execution, and customer comms under pressure. Conduct monthly for oncall teams and quarterly cross-functional drills with customer-success.

Sample 20-minute scenario (capacity blip):
- Minute 0: Alert fires (automated). Primary oncall acknowledges, opens channel.
- Minute 1–5: Triage metrics, hypothesis, and pick one immediate stabilizer.
- Minute 6–12: Apply mitigation (manual scale, route adjustments).
- Minute 13–18: Validate SLOs improving; prepare status page message.
- Minute 19–20: Close drill and capture 3 learning notes.

Exercise scoring rubric (pass/fail criteria)
- Pass if public message posted by T+15 and P95 improves by >=20% within 20 minutes.
- Partial if message posted but no measurable improvement.
- Fail if no message posted or escalation path not followed.

Post-incident: postmortem & remediation tracking

Trigger for postmortem: any capacity blip that meets either of:
- Customer SLA breached (credit threshold) OR
- Incident lasted >60 minutes OR
- Root cause unknown at time of resolution.

Postmortem template (blameless):
- Summary: one-paragraph high-level summary.
- Timeline: bullet list of events with UTC timestamps.
- Impact: services, customers, duration, and numbers (requests failed).
- Root cause analysis: short, medium, long causal chains.
- Corrective actions: owner, due date, verification criteria.
- Preventative actions: capacity rules, alert tuning, automation.
- Learnings and open questions.

Remediation tracker example (table text)
||Action||Owner||Due||Verification||
|Increase autoscaler headroom by 15%|Infra Capacity Lead|2026-03-15|Load test w/ 2x traffic|
|Add KV cache eviction alert at 60s rate|Runtime Owner|2026-02-20|Alert test via synthetic evictions|

Appendix: common safe operations and rollback principles

- Safe operations: non-disruptive config toggles (increase cache size), rate limiting low-priority background jobs, activating degraded routing. Always document the command, the reason, and expected effect before applying.
- Rollback guidance: prefer roll-forward when stateful changes are safe; for config changes that could impact correctness, prepare a tested rollback command.
- Change window policy: if mitigation requires >10% client-impacting change, coordinate with support and schedule outside business hours unless emergency.

Access checklist (for verification during onboarding)

- PagerDuty: verified
- GitOps: ability to apply runtime-config toggles (limited write access)
- Dashboards: read access to redwood-runtime, autoscaler, router-proxy
- Status page editor: access to post and update messages
